item.title: Stretched bilayer-cytoskeleton links hold echinocytes in a model splenic slit
item.description: arXiv:2611.16241v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Stored red blood cells become echinocytes, growing spicules before losing membrane; the spleen clears the resulting small, spherical cells. Whether spicules alone hinder splenic passage is unknown. Shape and area change together. In a two-component model whose shrinking cytoskeleton raises spicules, we drove a discocyte and stage I to III echinocytes of equal area and volume through a model splenic slit. The pressure drop needed to pass rose with stage; stage III echinocytes were held at 37 to 50 times the pressure drop that passed the discocyte. Bilayer-cytoskeleton links stretched near full extension held these cells; lengthening them about twofold released a held cell. Capillary-sized channels, as in our device, separated the stages far less. Of the shape classes in stored blood, the model held at high pressure drops only storage-induced microerythrocytes, which perfused human spleens clear most. Spicules, besides membrane loss, may decide which stored cells the spleen retains.
item.dc:creator: Zhaojie Chai, Jianlu Zheng, He Li, Ming Dao, George Em Karniadakis

item.title: Confinement Limits Cell Shape and Mitotic Pressure During Division
item.description: arXiv:2602.18909v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Cells often divide under mechanical confinement, where surrounding structures restrict shape changes during cytokinesis. We analyze a minimal model of a dividing cell as an incompressible volume bounded by an interface with effective isotropic tension, and show that confinement imposes a minimum attainable furrow radius. Beyond this limit, the cytokinetic ring can continue to contract within a septum without further furrow ingression, leaving the cell shape, mitotic pressure, and transmitted force unchanged. We determine this confinement-limited state for rigid parallel walls, soft axial confinement, and three-dimensional enclosures. Between parallel walls, the limiting force and minimum furrow radius collapse onto universal curves when scaled by surface tension and cell size. In soft confinement, environmental stiffness and spindle forces select the operating point. In three-dimensional confinement, the free volume between the cell and the confinement controls force transmission and cell shape. This yields a method for inferring the mechanical state of a cell dividing in deformable three-dimensional confinement from its shape. The radius and tangent angle of the cell surface at the stalled furrow and at the point where the cell detaches from its surroundings determine the mitotic pressure and the axial force carried by the cell surface, relative to the cortical tension.
item.dc:creator: Amit Singh Vishen
